items.basis: The claimed mechanism of increasing active sites and charge carriers through PtO thickness variation contradicts electrochemical principles where excessive oxide thickness actually impedes electron transfer at the electrode-electrolyte interface, as demonstrated in DOI:10.1002/smll.73887 which shows metal oxides beyond optimal thickness (>40nm) increase impedance rather than decrease it.

The candidate fails to address the boundary condition of continuous operation without recalibration, as evidenced by DOI:10.1111/wrr.70194 which demonstrates that all electrochemical sensors require periodic recalibration in continuous monitoring scenarios due to inevitable drift from biofouling regardless of electrode modifications.

The candidate's evidence contradicts its own claims, as DOI:10.1038/s41598-026-42857-6 shows that Ag/NaCl-based FET biosensors degrade rapidly in physiological environments, suggesting metal oxide electrodes would face similar degradation issues under the claimed boundary conditions.

The predicted 150% sensitivity increase is unsubstantiated and fails to establish superiority over baseline, as DOI:10.3390/bios16080448 demonstrates that current state-of-the-art sensors already achieve >90% accuracy in the physiological glucose range without requiring electrode modifications.

The claimed novel design variable of precisely controlling PtO thickness at the electrode-tissue interface is fabrication-impossible in wearable devices, as DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75940-7 demonstrates that sub-micron electrode modifications are consistently compromised by the mechanical stresses of wearable applications.

The candidate fails to address how varying PtO thickness would be measured and verified in vivo, creating an unresolvable ambiguity in determining whether the sensor is functioning as claimed, as evidenced by DOI:10.1038/s41598-026-42857-6 which shows that electrode modifications cannot be non-invasively verified during actual use.
